title: Deadly intentions trigger suicide by cop: Police the real victims when the desperate make them instruments of death
article: Insp. Paul Manuel of the Calgary Police Service was a young constable in 1982 when a crazed man with an axe came at him, ignoring officers' orders to drop the weapon.
Manuel, then 24, shot the man twice in the stomach. Karl Peter Freimanis, a 30-year-old petroleum industry engineer, died a few days later.
It was the first recognized case in Calgary of a phenomenon now widely known as "suicide by cop."
An internal police review and a fatality inquiry absolved Manuel of any blame in the incident.
Evidence indicated that Freimanis, who had a history of depression, was upset by an argument with his fiance.
On May 29, 1982, Freimanis told a friend over the phone that he had solved his problems "by killing somebody."

The friend called police, who quickly surrounded the Ranchlands home. When they arrived, they saw Freimanis inside talking on the telephone and holding a high-powered rifle in one hand. He turned with the rifle pointing at them and the officers took cover. Freimanis later came out of the house carrying a knife but went back inside. He emerged 20 minutes later carrying an axe.
One witness reported that Freimanis was "beckoning with one hand and holding the axe in the other."
In the days that followed the fatal incident, Brian Sawyer, then chief of police, told the media that Freimanis had appeared to use police as a "vehicle" to commit suicide.
Now nearly 19 years later, Manuel says he remembers the incident vividly but tries not to dwell on it.
"I haven't given it much thought in a long time," he said. "Of course I think about it, but I don't analyse it. It was just something that happened."
This past December, another Calgary police officer found himself ensnared in a suicide-by-cop scenario.

Most armed robbers plan to get away with their crimes. Not Arthur George Provencal. Provencal, 34, walked up to the prescription counter at a downtown pharmacy, pulled a large butcher knife and announced that he wanted to die. What happened next had all the markings of suicide by cop.

"Kill me, put me out of my misery," Provencal told the pharmacist after taking several hostages and demanding a lethal dose of injectable drugs. When the pharmacist refused, Provencal grabbed him from behind and pressed the blade of the butcher knife to his throat.

It was just before 6 p.m. on Dec. 23. Calgary's TD Square was bustling with last-minute Christmas shoppers as carols played over the mall's sound system. Moments later, a Calgary police officer inside the drugstore repeatedly ordered Provencal to drop the knife. When Provencal ignored the warnings, the officer fired a single shot from his 9-mm Glock handgun. The bullet struck Provencal in the head near the right eye. He was taken to hospital and pronounced dead.
But the "victim" in Provencal's death, says one expert who has studied this form of homicide, is the police officer who was compelled to pull the trigger.

"He's going to have to live with that for the rest of his life," said criminologist Rick Parent, a veteran police constable with the Delta Police Department in suburban Vancouver. "When people start talking about Christmas, he's going to be thinking about this violent scene and how he shot and killed this guy."

In a landmark study, Parent examined fatal police shootings in British Columbia from 1980 to 1994. He sifted through each case thoroughly in interviews with the police officers involved in the shootings as well as the friends and families of those who were killed.
His surprising conclusion was that in 10 per cent of the shootings, people had wanted police to kill them.

"In some of these cases, police were confronted in a calculated and deliberate manner by people who were suffering from one, or a combination of, suicidal tendencies, mental illness and substance abuse," Parent stated in his Master of Arts thesis on the subject of "victim-precipitated homicide."
"In many cases, suicidal individuals have engaged in life- threatening behaviour in order to force the police to kill them."

Provencal grew up in Ottawa and committed his first serious crimes there. At 21, he was charged with attempted murder after stabbing a teenager in a street confrontation. He pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of assault with a weapon and was sentenced to 20 months in jail.

When Provencal went into the Calgary drug store he was on statutory release from the medium-security Drumheller Institution, where he had served a sentence for armed robbery. For several months he had been reporting to a parole officer in Calgary.
He died with nothing in his pockets but a parole card.

This mandatory ID, which must be carried by parolees as a condition of their release, is like a membership card for the criminal class. But the way Provencal died -- apparently manipulating police into killing him -- makes him a member of a far more exclusive club: those who chose suicide by cop.
This past Wednesday there was another incident, in Washington, D.C. Police suspect the mid-day drama outside the White House was a suicide-by-cop attempt.

A former Internal Revenue Service employee fired several shots and waved his gun at police. He also put the barrel of the weapon in his mouth. Robert Pickett, 47, was arrested after a Secret Service agent shot him in the leg.

Such incidents are emotionally traumatic for the police officers involved, Parent learned, causing psychological effects including depression, guilt, nightmares, flashbacks and a heightened sense of danger and fear.

"Your mind can't cope with this," one officer told him. "Sleep? I'd wake up every night for several months. I would never relive the incident but my mind would focus on the incident." Another officer likened the flashbacks to "a video going on in your head that you can't control; it just keeps playing the video over and over and over again and you've got no control to turn it off."
Physical effects for some included loss of appetite and a marked decrease in sex drive.
"My sex life went down the tube, forget about that," said one officer. Several officers who were involved in a fatal shooting said their family life crumbled after the incident.

For some, the shooting became a family crisis. "My wife needed (psychological) help after the incident," said one officer. Another officer's wife developed an eating disorder. "We both know it was in response to me killing the guy," the officer related. "Even though it has been years since the shooting, she still suffers with the disorder and a few other things."
Another officer told Parent how he thought he was coping with the stress until his emotional well-being shattered six months after the fatal shooting incident.

"I thought everything was OK. It (the shooting) didn't bother me. I was tough. Then suddenly when I was out shopping with my wife and kids I had to park the car in the shopping centre. I had this urge to cry. I couldn't control it. Once I started I couldn't stop. My wife had to drive us home. It (the weeping) lasted for days."

The officer involved in December's shooting, who has not been publicly identified, received counselling and is now back at work. The police department's professional standards section and the internal affairs investigation unit worked with the homicide unit to complete an investigation into the incident. They found that the office responded appropriately given the circumstances.
An administrative review is now under way to determine if procedures should be changed.

Parent has also studied the "why" of suicide by cop. "It's difficult to take your own life," he said in an interview. "The best example is putting your hand in a fire. You may want to burn yourself, but you've got that physiological factor that forces you to pull your hand away. It's the same if you go to jump from a building or put a gun to your head. It's a lot harder to do, I think, than people imagine."
As well, he said, some people provoke police to shoot them to avoid the social or religious stigma of suicide.
"They may do it if they believe that if they die by someone else's hand they'll go to heaven, whereas if they kill themselves they'll go to hell."

But most cases fall into two main categories, he explained. "One is the hardened criminal who has done a lot of time and doesn't want to go back to jail. He feels that this is it, \`I've had a bad life and if I die I'm gonna go out in a blaze of glory. It's gonna be a Bonnie-and-Clyde type ending.'
"The other category is more the business or factory worker who has had a quiet life and wants some meaning to the way they die. This is their final statement, their swan song in getting out of life."

In Canada, about 10 people die each year at the hands of the police, compared with about 400 per year in the U.S., said Parent. A U.S. study that followed Parent's research methods found that slightly more than one in 10 fatal shootings by officers of the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department were suicide attempts. University of Southern California researchers looked at 437 officer- involved shootings from 1987-97. They found that suicide by cop accounted for 46 cases or 11 per cent of the total.

The study created a profile of those who decide to end their lives this way -- 98 per cent were men and 39 per cent of those had a history of domestic violence. Major characteristics included a past history of suicide attempts and a high incidence of alcohol and drug dependency.
The split second it takes for a cop to squeeze a trigger is "perhaps the mostly-widely seen and least understood event of our time," Parent concluded in a research paper.

"I think police get on the job thinking, \`It's not going to happen to me,' " Parent said in an interview. "And secondly, \`If it does happen to me, it's going to be clean and obvious and it's going to be a bad person like Clifford Olson. If I have to do it, it's going to be like I'm saving the day.' What you find is that it's not like that.

"It happens when you least expect it. It's extremely complicated, and maybe it's not a bad guy but somebody crying out for help. And due to circumstances you wind up killing him and it's messy, emotionally traumatic. It's like a roller-coaster ride. Most police don't expect that."

With growing awareness of the phenomenon, police are developing new strategies to better handle suicidal people they encounter, said Parent, including the use of Tasers, bean bag guns and other non- lethal weapons.
"Part of it is the research that's going on and part of it is the technology. They've developed a Taser now that's virtually 100-per- cent guaranteed to bring the person down without hurting them."

Police officers in Vancouver and its suburbs now carry Tasers, he said. "Not just the emergency response team, but average officers, too. So when they go to a call -- it may be a disturbance or a domestic -- they've got a Taser with them in their pocket. And if opportunity arises to use a less lethal weapon and they can, they have it right there to hand. So that's a good thing. Things are changing in the right direction."
But Parent, who has been a cop since 1980, notes that the police are virtually the only agency in western society that's available 24 hours of every day.
"Police are working all the time -- I worked New Year's Eve and Christmas -- and they go to basically anything and try to solve the problem whatever it is, social or criminal.

"It doesn't happen very often but sometimes police will come across something like a robbery or a murder in progress. And as they come into it they literally have 20 seconds to de-escalate the situation. And if the person wants to confront them, the officer doesn't have any choice but to kill them or to die himself.
"That's the only two choices."
